data.text:
Masks Against the Fire: NCR’s Unseen Battle

Dr Tony Leachon 

The fire at the Navotas landfill is more than a local incident. It is a stark reminder of how fragile our urban systems are, and how quickly environmental neglect can turn into a public health crisis.

For days, smoke and haze blanketed Metro Manila. The air turned acrid, visibility dropped, and residents were told to wear face masks outdoors. Not because of a pandemic this time, but because of toxic fumes from burning waste. The irony is painful: the very masks that once symbolized protection against COVID-19 are now shields against the consequences of poor waste management.

The impact on NCR has been immediate and far-reaching. Schools suspended outdoor activities, vulnerable groups were advised to stay indoors, and air quality monitors registered “unhealthy to very unhealthy” levels. What began in Navotas spread across the metropolis, proving that environmental disasters do not respect city boundaries.

But the deeper issue lies beneath the smoke. Landfills are not just repositories of garbage; they are symbols of systemic failure. When they burn, they release microplastics, heavy metals, and toxic chemicals into the air we breathe. They poison water sources through leachates. They erode trust in governance. And they expose the gap between policy promises and lived reality.

Wearing a face mask is a short-term defense. It protects lungs, but it does not solve the problem. The real solution requires accountability: stricter oversight of waste facilities, investment in sustainable disposal systems, and a commitment to protect public health over profit.

The Navotas fire is a warning. It tells us that the cost of neglect is borne not by corporations or officials, but by ordinary people—the commuters, the children, the elderly—who inhale the smoke and carry the burden of a system that refuses to change.

In the end, the question is not whether we should wear masks. The question is why we are forced to wear them at all.
